summary: Describes the changes between Unicode 6.0.0 and Unicode 12.0.0 as they affect IDNA2008, the standard for internationalized domain names. Because Unicode changes can alter what the IDNA2008 algorithm produces, it gives IANA the tables needed to match Unicode 12.0.0. It adds no exceptions. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When the list of letters from all languages grows, domain names need an updated list of allowed letters.

questions: what changed in unicode 12 for idna
what is u+111c9 sharada sandhi mark
what is a pvalid code point
subtitle: Why moving internationalized domain names from Unicode 6.0.0 to 12.0.0 needed no new exceptions, and what changed along the way.

tldr.problem: IDNA2008 calculates which characters are allowed in domain names from Unicode properties, so each new Unicode version can change the result, and IANA's tables had to be brought up to date.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews the changes between Unicode 6.0.0 and 12.0.0, finds one code point whose derived property value changed (U+111C9), and decides to add no exception rules. It gives IANA the tables for Unicode 12.0.0.
tldr.outcome: IDNA2008 stays as it is, the IANA registry was updated for Unicode 12.0.0, and later Unicode versions are reviewed under RFC 8753.

today: RFC 9233 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, and it covers only Unicode up to 12.0.0; later versions are to be reviewed under RFC 8753.

sections.title: The Problem with Moving Unicode Targets
sections.content:
IDNA2008 is the current version of Internationalized Domain Names for Applications. It includes an algorithm that calculates a derived property value for each code point from properties in the Unicode Standard. The values are defined in RFC 5892: PVALID (allowed in IDNs), CONTEXTJ and CONTEXTO (allowed only with specific context), DISALLOWED, and UNASSIGNED.

When Unicode is updated, new code points are assigned and properties of existing ones can change. A previously allowed code point may become disallowed, or the other way around. Earlier, three incompatible changes between Unicode 5.2.0 and 6.0.0 (U+0CF1, U+0CF2 and U+19DA) are described in RFC 6452, and the IETF decided not to update RFC 5892 for them.

This document covers Unicode 6.0.0 to 12.0.0. It also records the 2015 IAB statement about ARABIC LETTER BEH WITH HAMZA ABOVE (U+08A1), introduced in Unicode 7.0.0. The IETF added no exception for it, but the discussion led to RFC 8753, which clarifies the review process for new Unicode versions.
sections.eli5: Domain names may only use letters from an approved list. Whenever the big list of the world's letters gets new editions, someone has to check that the approved list still makes sense.

sections.title: IDNA2008 Documents and Deployment
sections.content:
IDNA2008 is a set of documents with informal names: Definitions (RFC 5890), Protocol (RFC 5891), Tables (RFC 5892), Bidi (RFC 5893), Rationale (RFC 5894) and Mapping (RFC 5895, which is advice only and not a required part of IDNA). The Unicode-based rules in RFC 5892 are expected to be stable across Unicode versions.

The RFC also lists the variations in use in the community, noting the list is not complete: IDNA2003 (RFC 3490 and RFC 3491, tied to Unicode 3.2), variations on IDNA2003, mixes of IDNA2003 and IDNA2008, the Unicode Technical Standard #46 approach, and the IDNA2008 algorithm applied to whatever Unicode version the operating system or libraries provide.

The Unicode Consortium assigns the maximum set of code points. IDNA2008 narrows that to the PVALID and CONTEXT sets, and DNS registries are expected to narrow further. SAC-084 and RFC 6912 recommend that registries be conservative and build their subsets by inclusion.
sections.eli5: Many people follow slightly different versions of the rulebook. The rules narrow things down in steps: all letters, then the letters allowed in domain names, then the smaller list each domain registry picks.

sections.title: Changes from Unicode 6.0.0 to 12.0.0
sections.content:
Most code points that change derived property value go from UNASSIGNED to PVALID or DISALLOWED. The RFC counts the characters in each category at each step; the total stays at 1114112, and CONTEXTJ (2) and CONTEXTO (25) never change.

  • 6.0.0 to 7.0.0: PVALID grew from 97418 to 99867. Nothing that impacts the calculation changed. U+17B4 and U+17B5 changed General Category but stayed DISALLOWED.
  • 7.0.0 to 10.0.0: PVALID grew from 99867 to 122411, with no code points changing derived property value.
  • 10.0.0 to 11.0.0: PVALID grew from 122411 to 122734, and one code point changed derived property value. Georgian letters had their General Category changed to Ll, but stayed PVALID. The new Mtavruli letters are uppercase and so DISALLOWED.
  • 11.0.0 to 12.0.0: PVALID grew from 122734 to 123006, with no code points changing derived property value.

Appendices A to F list every change between consecutive major versions.
sections.eli5: Over the years thousands of new letters were added, and almost all of them were simply added to the allowed or not-allowed pile. Only one old letter switched piles.

sections.title: The Sharada Sandhi Mark
sections.content:
The one incompatible change is U+111C9 SHARADA SANDHI MARK. Added in Unicode 8.0.0, it was first DISALLOWED. In Unicode 11.0.0 its General Category changed from Po to Mn and its Bidi property from L to NSM, so its derived property value became PVALID.

IDNA2008 allows adding rules to RFC 5892 (Section 2.7) in situations like this. The character is rarely used outside Sharada specialists, but is used in some records to mark sandhi breaks. The IETF could have added an exception or let the property value change. Because an exception would require implementation changes in deployments, and so that all sandhi marks are treated equally, it decided not to add a BackwardCompatible rule. Software based on Unicode older than 12.0.0 may still reject the character.
sections.eli5: One rare mark got moved from the 'not allowed' pile to the 'allowed' pile. Making a special exception would have meant changing lots of software, so the IETF let it move.

sections.title: Conclusion: No Exceptions
sections.content:
Considering deployment and the Unicode changes, including implications for normalization, the conclusion is not to add any exception rules to IDNA2008. This document addresses only Unicode 6.0.0 to 12.0.0. Future Unicode versions might lead to a different conclusion after the review process in RFC 8753, and the IETF might separately decide that RFC 5892 or other IDNA2008 documents need updates.

A stated objective is to make sure that a proper review of versions after 12.0.0 can be made.
sections.eli5: The answer is 'the rules still work, no special exceptions needed', with a promise to check again for later editions.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA updated the 'IDNA Rules and Derived Property Values' registry after the expert reviewer validated that the derived property values were calculated correctly. The appendices supply the tables for this. The document describes that IANA database as non-normative, with the IDNA2008 algorithm itself being the normative part.
sections.eli5: The official list of allowed letters was updated, and an expert checked that it was done right.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document makes recommendations about using the IDNA2008 algorithm for calculating derived property values, based on Unicode 12.0.0. It says nothing about future Unicode versions.

Not following the recommendations can lead to security issues. In particular, allowing confusable characters may lead to phishing attacks, as described in the Security Considerations sections of the IDNA2008 documents.
sections.eli5: If a domain name could use two letters that look the same, a trickster could make a fake website that looks real. Following the rules helps stop that.
